asSun.p: Libra's symbol is a pair of scales, and Justice is the one Major who's actually holding some, so with a Libra Sun there isn't much mystery about why this card is yours. Venus rules Libra. The awkward bit, and I always tell Libra Suns this early, is that the Sun is in fall in Libra. That's the old term for a planet sitting in the sign where it's least comfortable. The Sun wants to shine on its own terms, and Libra keeps asking what everyone else thinks. So your sense of who you are tends to come the long way round, through other people, through agreements, through seeing yourself in the person across the table. Libra is also cardinal air, and cardinal signs start things. People forget that about you. You don't wait for balance to turn up. You go and propose it, usually before anyone else has noticed anything was off.

Ask a Libra Sun what they want for dinner and you'll get a question back. That's the fall of the Sun in practice, and it's funny until it isn't. At work you can see exactly why the two people arguing in the meeting are both partly right, and you say so, and then somebody asks what you think and you find you've been so busy weighing that you haven't formed a view. At a family dinner you're the one who notices your sister's been talked over three times and quietly brings the conversation back to her. Choosing between two flats or two jobs, you make a spreadsheet, ignore it, then ask four friends. Underneath the dithering there's usually a decision already made. You just want to be sure it's fair before you say it out loud, and for you fair and true are close to the same word.

The gift nobody talks about is taste. Venus rules your Sun sign, and Libra's version of Venus is proportion, knowing something's right because it looks right. That covers a room, a sentence, a plan, a deal. You can read a contract and feel where it tilts before you've worked out why. I've seen a Libra Sun in a salary negotiation say almost nothing, just ask the one question that showed the offer was lopsided, and the number moved. You also make things fair without making them grim. A fight over who does the school pickup gets settled with a rota everyone actually likes, and somehow there's a joke in it. And the figure on the card holds a sword as well as the scales. When you do finally decide, you cut cleanly, and people are surprised how firm you can be.

Fairness can turn into a way of never being the one who wanted something. If every choice is made by weighing what's fair, you never have to own a desire. The holiday was chosen because it suited everyone. The job was taken because it made sense. Then some years in you realise you've built a life nobody could object to, and you're not sure it's yours. A quiet resentment comes with that, and it leaks. You keep a very accurate tally of who's given what, say nothing until the tally is huge, and then it all comes out in one polished speech, which your partner finds bewildering because you'd said everything was fine. With the Sun in fall, wanting things plainly is the actual practice for you. It doesn't come free, and it's worth the discomfort.

When something goes badly wrong, a Libra Sun's first move is to smooth it. You ring round, calm people down, make sure nobody's blaming anybody. After a redundancy you'll be reassuring colleagues in the car park before you've told your partner. A week later the fairness question arrives and gets a bit obsessive. Was it fair, whose fault was it, what should you have said, and you'll replay the conversation with the manager in the shower for days. The people around you get the tidy version of events and none of the anger, because anger feels ugly to a Venus-ruled Sun and you'd sooner be reasonable. That costs them, since they can tell something's being held back. What helps is letting yourself be unfair for an hour. Rant to one trusted person, take sides, say it wasn't right. Then go for a long walk.

Libra's natural house is the seventh, partnership, so for a Libra Sun love is close to where your sense of self gets made. You find out who you are partly by being with someone, and that's fine, it's how you're built. The risk is the slow blur, where two years in you like their music and their friends and can't remember what you used to order before you met. Aries is Libra's opposite sign, and a lot of Libra Suns end up with someone who has plenty of Aries in them, blunt, quick, happy to want things out loud. They're good for you. They show you, sometimes annoyingly, that asking for what you want isn't an act of aggression. Keep one thing that's entirely yours, a friendship, a sport, a Saturday morning, and don't put it up for negotiation.

You do your best work where there's something to balance. Law, HR, mediation, design, editing, diplomacy, any job where the pieces have to be made to fit. You like being the one who drafts the terms everybody can live with. Putting yourself forward is harder. The Sun in fall makes self-promotion feel crude, so you let the work speak and then watch someone louder take the promotion. What I'd say to any Libra Sun is that you're allowed to argue your own case with the care you'd give a colleague's. Write it up as though you were representing someone else, if that helps. You also need a workplace that plays fair. A boss with favourites wears you out in a way long hours never do, and you'll stay far too long trying to fix the culture single-handed.

At twenty a Libra Sun is often charming and a little shapeless, very good company, agreeing with whoever's in front of them, falling for people partly to find out who they are. The first big decisions get made by consensus and some of them turn out to have been other people's. By the mid-thirties there's usually been a reckoning, a relationship or a career chosen to keep the peace that had to be undone, and out of it comes a firmer person who can say 'no, I'd prefer this'. The sword starts getting used. The fifties tend to bring real authority. People trust your judgement because they've watched you arrive at it slowly and honestly for years. The thing to watch then is a certain primness, a habit of handing down verdicts on how other people live.

Once a day for a week, make one small decision without asking anyone and without explaining it. What to eat, which film, which way to walk home. Say it as a plain statement: 'I'd like Thai.' No 'if that's okay', no 'unless you'd prefer'. Notice how long the urge to soften it lasts, and whether anyone actually minds. Usually nobody does, and that's worth knowing in your body.

asMoon.p: The Moon is your feelings, what you need to feel safe, what you do at eleven at night when something's bothering you. In Libra it has no special dignity. It's a visitor, neither helped nor held back, and it takes on the colour of Libra's ruler, Venus. So your emotional life runs on Venus things. Harmony, company, a pleasant room, people being kind to each other. Justice is Libra's card, and as a Moon card it's about how you settle a feeling, which is by weighing it. Look at the figure on the card, sitting very still between two pillars with the scales level. That's the state you keep trying to get back to. Libra is an air sign too, so feelings reach you partly as thoughts, and you often don't know how you feel about something until you've talked it through with someone.

You feel other people's moods almost before your own. You walk into a friend's kitchen and know the couple has been arguing, and you spend the evening lightly making it better without anyone asking. A tense group chat keeps you up. When someone's cross with you, you can't really rest until it's sorted, and sorted means talked about properly, both sides, an understanding reached. Being left on read after a slightly sharp message is agony. Ugliness gets to you physically, whether it's a harsh voice, a messy room, or dinner eaten standing up at the bench. You can be happy on your own for a while, but give you a whole weekend without company and something in you starts to wilt by Sunday afternoon. And the films that make you cry are nearly always the ones about somebody being treated unfairly.

What you have is the ability to make a hard conversation feel safe. A Libra Moon can sit two furious people down at a kitchen table and have them both feeling heard inside half an hour. That's a real skill and not many people have it. The quieter gift is that you forgive properly once things have been made fair. If the other person has actually owned their part, you don't carry the old grudge. The friend who let you down badly last year, apologised and meant it, gets a clean slate, and they can feel that it's clean. You also make comfort lovely. Flowers when someone's ill, the right song at the right moment, a table laid carefully for a friend who's had a terrible week. With Venus colouring this Moon, care comes out of you as something beautiful, and people remember it for years.

You'll give up a need to keep the peace, and then feel it as a debt someone owes you. You wanted to stay in, you went to the party because your partner wanted to, and you were charming all night. Nobody knew. On the drive home you're quietly furious, and later that week it comes out about something else entirely, the dishes, the tone of a text. The other catch is that a Libra Moon wants feelings to be reasonable before they're allowed. If you can't justify being upset, you talk yourself out of it. Jealousy, envy, plain grumpiness, anything a bit ugly, gets argued down and filed away. It doesn't go anywhere. It turns up months later as a sadness you can't explain, or a sudden coolness towards someone who never knew they'd done anything.

Under strain a Libra Moon goes looking for someone to talk to, and then another someone, and then a third, to check the first two were right. After a break-up you'll have the whole story polished and even-handed within a day, including their side, which you'll explain better than they would. That's the airy way this Moon gets safe again. A week later the talking stops working and you go tired and flat. Decisions get hard, even small ones, and meals start getting skipped. The people around you find it difficult, because you keep telling them you're fine and you're very reasonable about it all. What actually helps is somewhere pleasant to be and someone who won't make you explain. A warm bath, clean sheets, a friend on the sofa watching rubbish with you, and no analysis at all.

You need a partner who's easy to be around, and you shouldn't be embarrassed about that. For a Libra Moon a relationship full of friction is exhausting in a way that goes past the bickering. The house has to feel good. You need to be spoken to kindly, even mid-argument, and you need things to feel roughly even, who cooks, who rings whose parents, who says sorry first. Cancer and Capricorn both square Libra, and you'll feel it if you fall for someone with a lot of either, very moody or very stern, because your need for calm keeps getting bumped. It can work. It just takes more saying out loud. The real risk for you is agreeing too early. Tell a new partner what bothers you within the first few months, while it's still small and easy to say.

Your feelings are the office thermometer. If there's a feud between two colleagues you'll know before management does, and within a week you'll be quietly carrying messages between them. That's useful, and it's also a lot of work nobody's paying you for. A Libra Moon does well in jobs with a decent atmosphere and some fairness built into them, a clear process, open salaries, a manager who deals with problems. Places that are ugly to be in, harsh strip lighting, open-plan shouting, a boss who humiliates people, get under your skin. Treat that as a real factor when you choose where to work, alongside the pay. And at the end of a hard day, check whether the upset you're carrying home is yours or something you picked up from someone else at lunch.

In the twenties a Libra Moon tends to live in other people's moods. You're the peacemaker in the share house, you go along with things, and you can't quite tell what you feel until a friend tells you. Relationships get chosen partly for how nice they feel, which is fine until it isn't. Through the thirties you usually learn that keeping the peace and being at peace are different jobs. Often it takes a relationship ending, or a friendship that turned out to be one-sided, to teach it. The fifties are often very good for this Moon. You can say something upset you without first building a case, and home has become a genuinely calm place, arranged just how you like it. The risk later on is a low tolerance for mess of any kind, including other people's grief.

When you notice you're upset and can't justify it, don't argue with it for once. Say it to yourself in one short line, out loud if you're alone: 'I'm jealous', 'I'm cross with them', 'I didn't want to go'. No reason attached. Then do one small Venus thing for yourself. Put on a song you love, or make the tea properly in a pot, and let the feeling sit there for ten minutes without fixing it.

asRising.p: Your rising sign is the one that was coming up on the eastern horizon when you were born, and it sets the first house, which covers your body, your manner and how you begin things. With Libra there, Venus becomes your chart ruler, so wherever Venus sits in your chart tells a lot of the story. Justice is Libra's card, and it's the card strangers meet. Libra being cardinal air, you open things socially. You're the one who does the introductions, suggests the plan, breaks the silence in the lift. Whole-sign houses put Aries on your seventh house, Cancer on your tenth and Capricorn on your fourth, and those three come up again and again in how a Libra rising lives. It's a chart that looks graceful from the front and has some quite hard-edged signs sitting behind it.

People tend to assume you're easy, and in the first ten minutes you are. At a job interview you match the panel's tone without thinking. At a wedding you get seated between the two relatives who don't speak, because someone sensed you'd cope. Strangers ask you for directions. In a shop you'll apologise when someone else bumps into you. You notice how a room's arranged, and you'll quietly move a chair so nobody's got their back to the group. You also start things by consulting. A new job, a new gym, a new neighbour, and your opening move is to find out how things are done here and who everyone is. It's graceful and it works. It can also mean people know your manners for years before they hear a single opinion of yours.

The less obvious gift is timing. Libra rising knows when to say something, which matters a great deal and gets very little credit. You can raise the awkward pay issue with your manager on exactly the right afternoon, in exactly the right tone, and get a yes. With Venus ruling the chart you also have a way of making other people look good. You introduce a shy friend at a party by mentioning the one thing they're proud of, and suddenly they're talking. Then there's the sword in Justice's hand, the part people miss. Behind the pleasant manner is someone who's clear about what's fair, and when a line gets crossed in front of you, a waiter being bullied, a colleague blamed for someone else's mistake, you say so. Politely, and it lands, because nobody saw it coming.

The mask can get stuck. Because you're so good at arriving pleasantly, you can go years without letting anyone see you annoyed, and people start taking the pleasantness as all there is. Then they're shocked the first time you object, and you're hurt that they're shocked. There's also a habit of reading everyone in the room and adjusting to all of them at once, which is tiring and leaves you unsure, driving home from the barbecue, which of the four versions of you was actually you. Libra rising can be vague about commitments as well. You say 'we should definitely do that' to six people a week, mean it at the time, and follow up with two. Nobody thinks you're rude. A few people quietly stop believing you, though, and it's worth knowing who they are.

When things go wrong your face stays pleasant, sometimes unnervingly so. You'll get the call about your father in the middle of a work lunch and finish the lunch. That's the rising sign holding the door shut. The first days are all manners, thanking people, answering messages, organising who brings what. A week or two later the body tends to complain. With Venus ruling the chart, strain often shows up as losing interest in the things that usually give you pleasure. Clothes, food, music, the lot. Friends might not clock it, because you still look put together. What helps is someone close who sees straight through the manners, and permission to be a bit graceless for a while. Cancel things. Wear the old jumper. Let the phone go to voicemail and don't ring back till you want to.

With Libra rising, Aries sits on your seventh house, the house of partners. So the people you're drawn to tend to be direct, a bit impatient, sometimes combative, the kind who says exactly what they want on the first date and has booked the second before you've finished your drink. That's attractive to you for good reason. They do the thing you find hardest. It's worth watching, though, that you don't end up handing them all the wanting, so they choose and you fit around it. Warmth is your default setting with strangers, which can come across as flirting when you didn't mean anything by it, and a partner may need that explained. Tell them early that it's just manners. Then show them the side of you nobody at the party gets to see.

Cancer falls on your tenth house, career and reputation. So for all the Libra polish at the door, the working life that tends to suit you has a caring or protective side to it. Looking after clients, running a team like a family, work in homes or food or health or schools. People come to see you publicly as someone who looks after things, and that reputation builds quietly over years. First impressions do a lot of the work in interviews and client meetings, and you should let them. The catch is that Cancer squares Libra, so the pull between being liked and being protective shows up at work. You'll find it hard to tell someone on your team the bad news they need to hear. Rehearse it once, say it kindly, and then stop softening it.

At twenty Libra rising is all charm and a bit of a people-pleaser. You're attractive in the way that comes from paying attention to how things look, you're asked to everything, and you say yes to most of it. Capricorn on your fourth house, home and family, often goes with a background that was serious or duty-heavy, and the lightness at the door was partly learned there. Through the thirties you usually start building a home of your own that's solid and well run, and people who only know the charm are surprised by it. That's the Capricorn fourth doing its work. The fifties bring a kind of earned elegance, a face that's been kind for a long time and shows it. What changes most is that you stop needing everyone at the party to like you. Two or three is plenty.

The next time a stranger or a new colleague asks what you think about something, give your actual opinion in the first sentence, before you've checked their face. Keep it short and friendly. 'I didn't like it much, to be honest.' Then stop, and let a second of silence go by before you soften anything. Do this three times over a week and notice who leans in.

asBirthCard.p: Birth cards come from the date alone, so this has nothing to do with your Sun or any other sign in your chart. You added up all the digits of your birthdate, reduced anything over 22, and landed on eleven. Eleven is built from two ones standing side by side, one person and another who's their equal, which is about as simple a picture of fairness as a number can give. It also sits in the middle of the Majors, just after the Wheel of Fortune and just before The Hanged Man. The Wheel is luck, things turning whether you like it or not. Justice is where luck stops being the explanation and your own choices start adding up. Then comes The Hanged Man, who stops and hangs there until he sees it differently. The card itself belongs to Libra, the scales, which says something about its nature and nothing about where your planets are.

As a pattern across a life, eleven tends to turn up as a run of moments where you're asked to be the fair one, and they aren't always comfortable. The friend who tells you both sides of the break-up and wants to hear they were right. The will that gets read out, and the siblings who all turn to look at you. The workplace where you see the manager's favouritism and you're the only one who'll mention it at the staff meeting. Small choices from years back keep coming home too, good and bad. The favour you did in your twenties that turns into a job offer at forty. The corner you cut once that somebody still remembers. People with this card often say their life feels oddly tidy in that way, as though it keeps its own books.

Beyond fairness, the real gift of eleven is that you're believable. Over a lifetime people learn that your account of events matches what happened, and that becomes a kind of capital. Your reference gets someone a job. When two relatives fall out, both of them will accept your version. I've seen elevens called in to referee things they had no official part in, a neighbour dispute, a club committee, a divorce where both people trusted them. The other gift is a calmness about consequences. Because you've watched cause and effect work so many times, you don't panic when something you did comes back to you. You say yes, that was me, and deal with it, which is surprisingly rare and makes people relax around you.

The less obvious shadow is keeping accounts where none should be kept. With eleven running through a life, it's easy to start treating love like a ledger. You rang last time, so they should ring. You paid for dinner twice. You remember who didn't come to your fortieth. None of it is wrong exactly, and the numbers are usually accurate, which makes them harder to let go of. The other trap is being so used to being the fair one that you can't stand being in the wrong. When you've made a real mistake, hurt someone or forgotten something that mattered, you'll go to great lengths to show it was understandable. Sometimes it was. Sometimes the fairest thing would be to say sorry and leave it there, with no explanation attached.

When life goes wrong for someone with this birth card, the first instinct is to find out why. Whose fault, what went wrong, which choice led here. After a loss you'll want the facts in order before you let yourself grieve, and the first week can go on forms and phone calls and timelines. Then it turns on you. A week or so in, the question shifts to what you did wrong, and you'll go over it at three in the morning looking for your part. The people around you find that hard to watch, because they can see it wasn't your doing and you're prosecuting yourself anyway. What helps is someone who knew the situation telling you, plainly, where your responsibility ended. Then a slow, physical day, a long walk or a swim, where nothing gets weighed.

In love an eleven wants to be met as an equal, and that runs deeper than splitting the bills. It's being consulted, being taken seriously when you disagree, having your word count for as much as theirs. You'll put up with a lot in a relationship but not with being talked down to. The less obvious thing is that you tend to fall for people you respect before you fall for people who excite you. That's a good way to choose, and it can leave you wondering, years in, where the fizz went. Some elevens need to learn to be a little unreasonable in love, to want someone for no fair reason at all. And when there's a row, you're good at seeing both sides. Try staying on your own side for a minute first.

Elevens do well anywhere the job is making a fair call. Judges and referees, obviously, but also editors, auditors, teachers marking essays, managers doing reviews, anyone setting prices or writing rules. You're good at the part everyone else avoids, which is giving someone the honest assessment in a way they can take. Your career also tends to be built out of reputation, slowly. The work you did properly years ago brings the next job, and people remember if you ever took credit that wasn't yours. That's worth keeping in mind on the dull days. The risk at work is becoming the office conscience, the person everyone brings problems to, who ends up fixing things that were never theirs to fix. Say where your job ends, and say it early.

In your twenties an eleven is often quite fierce about fairness, quick to call things out, a bit self-righteous sometimes, and very hard on friends who fall short. The consequences of early choices haven't arrived yet, so it's all principle. By the mid-thirties they have. You've seen choices you made at twenty-two come back, some as blessings and some as bills, and your idea of justice gets humbler and a lot more practical. This is often when an eleven stops judging and starts mediating. The fifties tend to bring the part of the card that's easy to miss, the veil hanging behind the figure, and with it the sense that you never see the whole of anyone's story. Elevens at that age are usually the ones handing out second chances, and they're seldom wrong about who deserves one.

Pick one relationship where you've been keeping score, the friend who never rings first, the sibling who owes you. For a month, do one generous thing for them each week without counting it. Ring first. Pay for the coffee. Don't mention it and don't tally it afterwards. If you catch yourself adding it up, and you probably will, say 'off the books' in your head and let it go.
